e-5922.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace
e-5922.problem:
Find the distance between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/faad91efe9dd5872c09b3dc05dbdb333a1180880e1f072062c4b1f74e5754e61.png)
e-5922.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In our case, we have 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/60ff5bf60ca0505446961f9bfae83d1ece21d53cd180fdd6a687dba1ca767b68.png)

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 8 & 18\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3-(-3))^{2}+(5-5)^{2}+(-1-1)^{2}+(3-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+0+4+4} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9906.knowledge_point: Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace
e-9906.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\},$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/2c71360d859e203a5e1533b3c9aaa91c11243c1eba0bca05f92a03378850b067.png)
e-9906.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In our case, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/9cdf7153834225217e3cfd680182777f47f2cc0d09185a66742b46fc67ebd7b6.png)
Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -3 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -3 \\ 3 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}27 & 9 \\ 9 & 27\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ -3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/4e59afb848b5180340b05874c2dd63d04c22186c0c8e2235535e19551cab983a.png)

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+0\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta = \arccos\left( \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}2\right)= \dfrac\pi 4,
$$

which is already an acute angle, as desired.

e-5923.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto the Solution Space of a Linear System
e-5923.problem:
Given the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system.
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/043050d4ab229a40aef87d4a404f5af2337a36d1ba54926dcb9a214fdad5e245.png)
e-5923.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2,$ and $x_3$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get $x_1 = 2x_2-3x_3.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/8aac548229fb8312eefaed282dd27daadf560b17009f163d568ca1edda949a69.png)

Consequently, 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070757/assets/b241f88f83f96ef2f393b7450e5933831b300b98522b16b02208298db1b4ea91.png)
is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we let $A$ be a matrix whose columns equal the elements of $\mathcal B,$ and we find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ -6 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 8 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx. In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[1−1001100]⟹AT=[1010−1010].

Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[1−1001100]⋅([10−10−1010]⋅[1−1001100])−1⋅[10−10−1010]⋅[2354]=[1−1001100]⋅[2002]−1⋅[73]=[1−1001100]⋅12[1001]⋅[73]=[1−1001100]⋅[7232]=[2050]=x^

Finally, the distance between x and the subspace S is given by d(x,x^)=‖x−x^‖=(x1−x^1)2+(x2−x^2)2+(x3−x^3)2+(x4−x^4)2=(2−2)2+(3−0)2+(5−5)2+(4−0)2=0+9+0+16=25=5.

content.problem:
Find the distance between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2-2)^{2}+(3-0)^{2}+(5-5)^{2}+(4-0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+9+0+16} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}

after.problem:
Find the distance between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].

after.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3-2)^{2}+(-3-(-1))^{2}+(0-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4+4} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}

$$

content.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3-2)^{2}+(-3-(-1))^{2}+(0-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4+4} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx. In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[01−101100]⟹AT=[0−1101010].

Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[01−101100]⋅([0−1101010]⋅[01−101100])−1⋅[0−1101010]⋅[0031]=[01−101100]⋅[2112]−1⋅[33]=[01−101100]⋅13[2−1−12]⋅[33]=[01−101100]⋅[11]=[1−120]=x^

Finally, the distance between x and the subspace S is given by d(x,x^)=‖x−x^‖=(x1−x^1)2+(x2−x^2)2+(x3−x^3)2+(x4−x^4)2=(0−1)2+(0−(−1))2+(3−2)2+(1−0)2=1+1+1+1=4=2.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace
content.problem:
Find the distance between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0-1)^{2}+(0-(-1))^{2}+(3-2)^{2}+(1-0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Find the distance between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-17 \\ -14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{15}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-17 \\ -14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(5-3)^{2}+(5-6)^{2}+(1-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: A normal to the plane is n=(1,-2,-1), orthogonal to both spanning vectors. The acute angle θ with the plane satisfies sin(θ)=|x·n|/(||x|| ||n||)=3/(3√6)=1/√6. Thus θ=arcsin(1/√6)≈24.09°.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
after.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}11 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}8 & -8 \\ -8 & 11\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 5+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{15}{\sqrt{9}\sqrt{30}} \\  & =\frac{15}{3\sqrt{30}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{5}{\sqrt{30}})≈{24.09}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 5 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+0\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{4},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

decision.explanation: The normal vector n=(1,1,0) is orthogonal to both spanning vectors. The angle θ with the plane satisfies sin(θ)=|x·n|/(||x|| ||n||)=9/(√54·√2)=√3/2. Therefore θ=π/3.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 6 & 27\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}27 & -6 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{(-6)\cdot (-3)+(-3)\cdot 3+3\cdot 6}{\sqrt{(-6)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{3}^{2}}\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{3}^{2}+{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{27}{\sqrt{54}\sqrt{54}} \\  & =\frac{27}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
after.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,3\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$ 

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+1\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot (-4)}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{24}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{3\cdot 8}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{8}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{8}}{3})≈{19.47}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

decision.explanation: The vector n=(1,0,-1) is orthogonal to both spanning vectors. The acute angle θ with the plane satisfies sin(θ)=|x·n|/(||x|| ||n||)=2/(√14·√2)=1/√7. Therefore θ=arcsin(1/√7)≈22.21°.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
after.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$   

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{12}} \\  & =\frac{12}{2\sqrt{42}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{6}{\sqrt{42}})≈{22.21}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

decision.explanation: Both equations reduce to x1=x3, so the solution space consists of (t,s,t). Orthogonal projection averages the first and third coordinates and preserves the second, giving (1,2,1). The residual (-1,0,1) is orthogonal to this solution space.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to its row echelon form. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to its row echelon form. Then

M=[20−2040−40]R2:=R2−2R1∼[20−200000]. In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2,x3 are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get x1=x3. Therefore, the general solution is [x3x2x3]=x2[010]+x3[101],x2,x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[010],[101]} is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of x onto the solution space of the system: projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx=[011001]⋅([010101]⋅[011001])−1⋅[010101]⋅[022]=[011001]⋅[1002]−1⋅[22]=[011001]⋅12[2001]⋅[22]=[011001]⋅[21]=[121]

verification.explanation: The solution space is {(t,s,t)}. The vector (1,2,1) lies in it, and the residual (0,2,2)−(1,2,1)=(-1,0,1) has zero dot product with every (t,s,t). This verifies the orthogonal projection and agrees with the worked solution.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto the Solution Space of a Linear System
content.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to its row echelon form. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Both equations require x1=2x3, giving the solution space {(2t,s,t)}. Projecting (5,5,0) onto the orthogonal basis (2,0,1), (0,1,0) gives (10/5)(2,0,1)+5(0,1,0)=(4,5,2).

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[550],{x1−2x3=02x1−4x3=0

a

b
 [424]
c

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[10−2020−40]R2:=R2−2R1∼[10−200000]. In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2,x3 are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get x1=2x3. Therefore, the general solution is [2x3x2x3]=x2[010]+x3[201],x2,x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[010],[201]} is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of x onto the solution space of the system:

projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx=[021001]⋅([010201]⋅[021001])−1⋅[010201]⋅[550]=[021001]⋅[1005]−1⋅[510]=[021001]⋅15[5001]⋅[510]=[021001]⋅[52]=[452]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto the Solution Space of a Linear System
content.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 14\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-9{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -9 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto the Solution Space of a Linear System
content.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 14\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-9{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -9 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[−52−5],{x1−2x3=0−2x1+4x3=0

a
[63−2]
b
[26−3]
c
[−62−3]
d
[−32−6]
e
[2−3−6]
Submit

decision.explanation: Both equations define the plane with normal n=(1,0,-2). The projection is x−((x·n)/(n·n))n=(-5,2,-5)−(5/5)(1,0,-2)=(-6,2,-3).

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -15\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -15\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[−52−5],{x1−2x3=0−2x1+4x3=0

a
[63−2]
b
[26−3]
c
[−62−3]
d
[−32−6]
e
[2−3−6]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[10−20−2040]R2:=R2+2R1∼[10−200000]

In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2,x3 are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get x1=2x3. Therefore, the general solution is [2x3x2x3]=x2[010]+x3[201],x2,x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[010],[201]} is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of x onto the solution space of the system: projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx=[021001]⋅([010201]⋅[021001])−1⋅[010201]⋅[−52−5]=[021001]⋅[1005]−1⋅[2−15]=[021001]⋅15[5001]⋅[2−15]=[021001]⋅[2−3]=[−62−3]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto the Solution Space of a Linear System
content.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -15\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -15\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get $3{x}_{1}=4{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{{x}_{3}}{3}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 25\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 25\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}25 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 25\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto the Solution Space of a Linear System
content.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get $3{x}_{1}=4{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{{x}_{3}}{3}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 25\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 25\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}25 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 25\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
